name: Adam Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Shah Accountancy, seven of us above a sari shop on the old parade. Most clients are family businesses: corner shops, two restaurants, a builder, a printing firm, and the community centre's accounts. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, mostly the same clients every year, so I know their kids' names. Mr Shah, who everyone calls Uncle Raj even though he's not my uncle, still likes clients to come in and sit down. What wears me out is chasing paperwork from people who keep receipts in a biscuit tin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Priya, who works as a pharmacy assistant, and the wedding's next August. I still live with my parents, and I help with their mortgage because my dad's shop hours were cut last year. So I've got almost nothing saved, maybe three weeks of my own costs. I don't use AI. I've got my calculator, my software and my files, and I trust what I can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Business is about trust, and you can't build trust with a chatbot. I'd say that to clients and to Uncle Raj, and at the community centre if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be stretched. AI being hype doesn't change that I'm paying towards my parents' mortgage and a wedding on a lower-paid job. That's a family worry, not a technology one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my clients happy, because they're my job security. I'd ask Uncle Raj for a few more clients so I can earn a bit more. And I'd try to save something small for the wedding each month, even thirty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. But I'd sleep fine about the work itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think clients would stay loyal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I sat with the builder when his tax bill came in and helped him set up a payment plan. You don't forget that. My clients come to me because they know me, not because I'm the cheapest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée Priya would say the same as her mother: a wedding is one day and a marriage is forty years. Priya's more sensible than me. She'd happily have a smaller wedding, it's our parents who want three hundred guests.

say: AI was hype, because **business is trust** and chatbots can't build it.
He'd say so to clients, **Uncle Raj** and at the community centre.
think: He's still stretched by his **parents' mortgage** and a coming wedding.
His worry is **family money**, not technology.
do: Keep **regular clients** happy as his main job security.
Ask Uncle Raj for **a few more** clients.
Save **thirty a month** towards the wedding.
feel: Uneasy about **money**, but sleeping fine about the work.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't change that I'm paying towards my parents' mortgage and a wedding on a lower-paid job.
fieldNote: Adam's job feels safe to him here, but **family costs** keep him uneasy.
He trusts **relationships** over technology and sees loyalty as protection.
His fiancée is more relaxed about the **wedding size** than their parents.

steps.text: Keep looking after the same family-business clients at Shah Accountancy
Save thirty pounds a month towards the August wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool, and good firms will use it carefully. People will still want someone they trust to sign their accounts. I'd say the market will sort out the good from the bad, and I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd worry. I'm the one at Shah Accountancy who doesn't use these things, and if Uncle Raj's son takes over, he loves gadgets. The young clients would go to cheaper online services, and the older ones would retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the bookkeeping for my dad's shop and my cousins' takeaway in the evenings, for a small fee, to bring in extra. I'd talk to Priya about a smaller wedding, maybe a hundred and fifty guests. And I'd keep my clients close, ring them before deadlines, the personal touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like feeling that the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts it out. What if it sorts you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that's fair, I suppose, as long as I had a fair chance. I don't want a handout. I'd want an apprenticeship or a course I could do while working, and my family behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I know. But I'd do it slowly, on my own clients first, checking everything twice. I've seen a client's online software put a car purchase down as a staff party.

say: AI is a **tool**, and good firms will use it **carefully**.
The **market** will sort good firms from bad.
think: He's the one at Shah who **doesn't use** the tools.
If **Uncle Raj's son** takes over, the firm could change fast.
do: Do **paid bookkeeping** for his dad's shop and cousins' takeaway.
Agree with Priya on a **smaller wedding** of 150 guests.
Ring clients before deadlines to keep the **personal touch**.
feel: Anxious, feeling the **ground move** under him.
S1.quote: I don't want a handout. I'd want an apprenticeship or a course I could do while working, and my family behind me.
fieldNote: Adam fears being the **least modern** person in a firm that might change hands.
He'd accept the **market's judgement**, provided he gets a fair chance.
He turns to **family businesses** for extra income, not public support.

steps.text: Do evening bookkeeping for his dad's shop and cousins' takeaway
Cut the wedding guest list from 300 to 150
Ring each client personally before their tax deadline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down. Companies and governments are rushing something nobody understands. I'm not one for regulation usually, but I'd say even the market needs time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone. Every bit of it is thinking work, and AGI would do it cheaper. My dad's shop would last a bit longer because someone has to stack shelves until the robots come in 2031, but that's not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Priya and both families and postpone the wedding by a year, maybe two. I'd ask my dad if I could help run the shop properly, do the ordering and look at opening longer hours. And I'd lean on family, because that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about my dad. My dad came here with nothing and built that shop, and here I am with a degree and it's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya's parents about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that I can't promise a job in two years. Priya's father would respect that more than me pretending. He's a practical man, he ran a fabric stall for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the shop in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's when the robots come for the shelves and the till, I suppose. By then maybe we'd have found something else. Or maybe people will still want a shopkeeper who knows them. I don't know.

say: Companies and governments are **rushing** something nobody understands.
He's not usually for regulation, but says even **the market** needs time to adjust.
think: His job goes, because it's **all thinking work**.
His dad's shop lasts until robots in **about 2031**, but isn't a career.
do: Postpone the **wedding** by one or two years.
Help run his **dad's shop**, handling ordering and longer hours.
feel: Alarmed, and pained that his **degree** would be worth nothing.
S2.quote: My dad came here with nothing and built that shop, and here I am with a degree and it's worth nothing.
fieldNote: Adam expects to **lose his job**, so alarmed, but family support keeps him short of panic.
He'd **postpone the wedding**, a big step for him and two families.
The **shop** is a hands-on bridge that lasts about three more years.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding with Priya by one to two years
Help run his dad's shop, taking over ordering
Move his costs onto the family household while he looks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who are willing to work. Learn a trade, start a business, support your family. I'd say that to younger lads at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I'd keep the job for maybe three, then it starts slipping. I'm not quick with new things, so I'd fall behind first. I'd have time to plan, but I'm not sure I'd plan well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next August as planned, but small, at the community centre. I'd start saving properly, fifty a month, and keep doing the books for family businesses. And I'd take Uncle Raj's offer to learn the new software, slowly, because I'd need it for a few years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed but quieter. Losing my job in five years feels like knowing a storm is coming next week, not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry on schedule in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years is enough to get on our feet as a couple. Priya's job is at the pharmacy counter, people-facing, so it has more time than mine. Two incomes for even a few years is better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when the job starts slipping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into my dad's shop full time and help grow it. Maybe a second shop. My dad always wanted a second shop, and by then I'd know enough about money to do it carefully.

say: Five years is enough for people **willing to work**.
He'd tell young men to learn a **trade** or start a business.
think: He'd keep the job **about three years** before it slips.
As someone **slow with new things**, he'd fall behind first.
do: Marry next August **as planned**, but small, at the community centre.
Save **fifty a month** and keep family bookkeeping going.
Learn the new **firm software** slowly with Uncle Raj.
feel: Alarmed but quieter, like a **storm** coming next week.
S3.quote: Losing my job in five years feels like knowing a storm is coming next week, not tomorrow.
fieldNote: Adam still expects to **lose the job**, so his mood stays alarmed.
Priya's **people-facing** job gives the couple more time, so the wedding goes ahead.
His long-term plan is growing his dad's **shop**, a family path.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding at the community centre next August
Save fifty a month alongside family bookkeeping
Learn Shah Accountancy's new AI software slowly with Uncle Raj

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair notice, and anyone who can't adjust in ten years has only themselves to blame. That sounds harsh, but it's what I believe. I'd also say families should start planning together now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years feels fine for a while. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with children by then. I'd keep my job for most of it, and I'd have time to build up my dad's shop as the backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Shah Accountancy as normal. I'd save for the wedding and then for a house deposit, slowly. And I'd wait and see for a few years, because I'm not changing everything on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the background. I'd notice it most when I think about children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thought about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to have it easier than me. In this picture, I'd tell them to learn something with their hands and their heart, like nursing or a trade. My mum would say I'm being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who can't adjust have themselves to blame. Would you include yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd have to. If I waited ten years and did nothing, that's on me. It's a bit frightening saying that out loud, because I know I'm slow to move.

say: Ten years is **fair notice**, and people who can't adjust must own it.
think: Ten years feels **fine for a while**, with his job lasting most of it.
His **dad's shop** is the backup he'd build up.
do: Keep working at **Shah Accountancy** as normal.
Save for the wedding, then a **house deposit**.
**Wait and see** a few years before changing anything.
feel: Anxious in the **background**, strongest when he thinks of **children**.
S4.quote: If I waited ten years and did nothing, that's on me.
fieldNote: Adam applies his **self-reliance** view to himself and admits it frightens him.
Ten years lets him **delay**, which suits a resistant person but carries risk.
He still expects his **accounting job** to go eventually, so anxious fits.

steps.text: Keep doing family-business accounts at Shah Accountancy
Save for a house deposit after the wedding
Wait a few years before deciding on a career change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit the wedding, my parents and my job all at once. What would help is a proper apprenticeship scheme for adults, paid, so a man can learn a trade and still support his family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about trust. My clients sign their names on accounts that I prepared, and I don't know if they'd sign under a machine's work the same way. They trust me with that signature.

headlineQuote: My clients sign their names on accounts that I prepared, and I don't know if they'd sign under a machine's work the same way.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** accountant at a seven-person family-run firm serving **local family businesses**.
He lives with his parents, helps with their **mortgage**, and is marrying Priya next August.
He doesn't use AI and **trusts** what he can check by hand.
He favours **self-reliance** and family over handouts, and applies that standard to himself.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed**, with his dad's **shop** as the fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting the wedding, his parents and his **job** at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** scheme so he can learn a trade and support family.
